title: Mr. Grubb Makes an Offer

pages.text:
The next morning, the rain had stopped, but the sky remained a heavy, bruised purple. The air in Saltmarsh Harbor felt thick, like trying to walk through cold honey. Juno pulled her yellow raincoat tighter, the fabric stiff with dampness. She clutched the spiral shell whistle in her pocket, feeling its smooth curve against her thumb. Beside her, Teo adjusted his round glasses, his messy black hair sticking up despite his green cap. He looked like he had slept in his shoes.

They walked past the silent fish market. The stalls were empty, the ice long melted into grey slush. The smell of old fish and wet rot hung in the air, a scent that made Juno’s stomach turn. She missed the clean, salty smell of the ocean, the kind that meant life was moving. Here, the water was stagnant, trapped in the mud, refusing to breathe.

A crowd had gathered outside the market. It wasn’t a friendly crowd. They stood in small, tight clusters, their shoulders hunched against the chill. Their faces were tired, lined with worry. They looked at the muddy harbor, then at each other, then back at the harbor. The silence was louder than the rain had been.

Juno stopped near the front, peering through the gap in the crowd. She saw Mayor Pruitt, jolly and tired, holding a half-eaten doughnut. He looked smaller than usual, his smile thin and brittle. Next to him stood a man in a shiny grey suit. He was tall and thin, with a tiny mustache that seemed to vibrate with impatience. His shoes were polished to a mirror shine, reflecting the grey mud around him.

Juno’s heart skipped a beat. She recognized the man. She had seen him in the bakery yesterday, looking at the bakery’s sign with the same hungry look he now gave the harbor. He was the one who had offered to buy the land.
pages.image: A rainy, grey street scene with a small crowd of worried townspeople standing outside a closed fish market. In the center, a tall thin man in a shiny grey suit stands out, his polished shoes reflecting the wet pavement, while a mayor with a doughnut looks nervous nearby.

pages.text:
The double doors of the fish market groaned open. Warm light spilled out onto the wet cobblestones, carrying the scent of frying onions and old wood. The crowd parted, not out of respect, but out of curiosity. They wanted to see who would speak.

Mr. Grubb stepped out first. He brushed an invisible speck of dust from his lapel, his movements precise and cold. He didn’t look at the people. He looked at the harbor. He looked at the boats stuck in the mud. His eyes were like pieces of cold glass, scanning the damage, calculating the cost.

"Good morning," he said. His voice was smooth, like oil poured over stone. It didn’t belong in this place of mud and rust. "I trust you’ve all been waiting for me."

Mayor Pruitt stepped forward, his doughnut crumbled in his hand. He looked like he wanted to run away, but his feet were rooted. "Mr. Grubb. We... we were hoping you could help."

"Help is a generous word," Grubb said. "I prefer solutions. The harbor is dead. The tide is gone. The boats are rotting. This is not a problem that can be fixed with hope and prayer. It is a problem that needs capital."

Juno felt a chill that had nothing to do with the weather. She looked at Teo. He was staring at Grubb’s hands. They were clean, manicured, and completely empty.

"What do you want?" someone asked from the back of the crowd. It was an old woman with a shawl wrapped tightly around her neck.

Grubb smiled. It did not reach his eyes. "I want to buy the land. All of it. The harbor, the shops, the lighthouse. For a price that will put food on your tables and jobs in your hands. In exchange, you let me build what this town needs. Progress."
pages.image: Mr. Grubb, tall and thin with a tiny mustache, stands in the doorway of a fish market, his hands clasped in front of him. He looks down at a crowd of small, worried figures, his expression cold and detached, contrasting with the warm, chaotic light spilling from behind him.

pages.text:
A murmur rippled through the crowd. It wasn’t anger, not yet. It was the low, rumbly sound of a stomach growling. Of fear. Of hunger.

Juno heard a voice, dry and cracked, from the left. Grandpa Ozzie.

The old man pushed his way through the crowd. He was tall, though he seemed to shrink when he walked. His bushy white beard was wild, and his blue knitted hat was slightly askew. He leaned heavily on his driftwood cane, his bad left knee protesting with every step. Biscuit, the fat orange cat with the chewed left ear, was perched on a crate nearby, watching the scene with one unblinking yellow eye.

"Ozzie," Mayor Pruitt said, his voice softening. "Sit down, Ozzie. You don’t have to stand."

"I’m fine," Grandpa said. He looked at Grubb, and for a second, his eyes were sharp. "You want the lighthouse, Mr. Grubb?"

Grubb’s smile tightened. "The lighthouse is part of the package. It’s a beautiful piece of history. We would preserve it. Turn it into a luxury guest house. Mini-golf on the grounds."

"Mini-golf," Juno whispered. The words felt ridiculous in her mouth. How could anyone think of mini-golf when the sea was dying?

Grandpa Ozzie took a step forward. He raised his hand, as if to point at Grubb, to say something important. Something that would stop this. His face was flushed, his eyes bright with emotion. He opened his mouth.

But then, his eyes went distant. He blinked. He looked around, confused. "Yes," he said softly. "Yes, that’s right. Mini-golf. Very good for the community."

The crowd sighed. It was a heavy, tired sound.

Juno’s heart sank. She knew that look. It was the look Grandpa got when the world was too loud, too fast, too much. He forgot. He always forgot when it mattered most.
pages.image: Grandpa Ozzie, tall with a bushy white beard and blue hat, stands in the middle of the street, looking confused and lost. He holds a driftwood cane, and behind him, the crowd of townspeople looks down, disappointed and weary.

pages.text:
Grubb nodded, satisfied. "Excellent. We can have the contracts drawn up by the end of the week. The Grand Low is in nine days. After that, the value of the land drops. You know this. I know this. We are all practical men."

Practical men. Juno’s hands curled into fists. She wanted to scream. She wanted to throw the shell whistle at his shiny shoes. She wanted to say that the sea wasn’t dead, it was sleeping. That it was waiting.

But she was quiet. She remembered Barnacle’s words. Do not let it hear you think.

Teo tugged her sleeve. "Juno," he whispered. His voice was tight. "Look at his pocket."

Juno looked. Grubb was checking his watch, a large, gold thing that gleamed in the grey light. As he moved, something caught in the pocket of his shiny grey suit. It was a glint of brass. Not gold. Brass. And it wasn’t a watch. It was a gear. A single, toothed gear, shiny and new.

Juno’s breath caught. She had seen that shape before. In the log. In the drawing of the Tide Clock.

It was the Moon Gear.

He had it. The man who wanted to build mini-golf had the missing piece of the machine that kept the sea alive.

"Mr. Grubb," Juno said. Her voice was small, but it cut through the air. "What is that in your pocket?"

Grubb looked down. He froze. For a second, his face was a mask of shock. Then, the coldness returned. He touched the pocket, and the gear disappeared.

"Nothing," he said. "Just a coin."
pages.image: A close-up of a shiny brass gear tooth peeking out from the pocket of a grey suit. The background is blurred, showing the muddy street and the legs of the crowd, focusing entirely on the metallic glint and the texture of the fabric.

pages.text:
"Coin," Teo repeated, his voice flat. He stepped forward, his tool belt clinking softly. "That’s not a coin, Mr. Grubb. Coins are round. That was a gear."

Grubb’s eyes narrowed. He looked at Teo, then at Juno. He didn’t look angry. He looked amused. Like a cat watching a mouse.

"You children are imaginative," he said. "But imagination doesn’t pay for the roof repairs. It doesn’t fix the nets. It doesn’t bring the tide back." He turned to the crowd. "I’ll have my lawyer call you. For now, I suggest you go home. It’s getting late. And the mud is getting deeper."

He turned and walked back into the fish market. The doors closed behind him with a heavy thud.

The crowd didn’t move. They stood in the silence, looking at the closed doors. Then, slowly, one by one, they turned and walked away. They didn’t look at Juno. They didn’t look at Teo. They just walked, their boots sinking into the grey slush.

Grandpa Ozzie was still standing there. He looked at Juno, and for a second, his eyes were clear. "Juno," he said. "What did he have in his pocket?"

Juno looked at the closed doors. She looked at the mud. She looked at Teo, who was staring at the ground, his jaw tight.

"He has the gear, Grandpa," Juno said. "He has the Moon Gear."

Grandpa’s face fell. He leaned on his cane, his shoulders slumping. "Oh," he said. "Oh, no."

The rain began to fall again, a fine, cold mist that settled on their shoulders. The harbor was silent. The sea was gone. And the clock was ticking.
pages.image: Juno, with curly dark-brown hair in two puffs and a yellow raincoat, stands in the rain, looking up at the closed fish market doors. Beside her, Teo with round glasses and a green cap looks down at the wet pavement, their expressions serious and worried.

summary: Mr. Grubb offers to buy the harbor land for a mini-golf resort, and Mayor Pruitt is tempted by the promise of financial stability. Grandpa Ozzie tries to object but forgets his argument, revealing his confusion. Juno spots the missing Moon Gear caught in Grubb's pocket, confirming he has stolen the key part of the Tide Clock.
